finding.claim: deleteAccount ignores the result of canDelete(u, a), so any caller can delete any account by id. The ownership/admin check is computed and discarded, and the delete at line 23 runs unconditionally. Its sibling closeAccount (line 29) uses assertCanDelete, which throws, so the two endpoints enforce different rules.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled `id` path parameter on DELETE /accounts/{id} (comment at line 19). Any caller who can reach this method with a User object, including a non-admin user owning no accounts, can supply an arbitrary account id.
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at src/AccountService.java:23 (destructive, unauthorized delete of another user's account).

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) takes the caller and the attacker-chosen id.
a = accounts.get(id) loads any account by id with no owner/tenant scoping.
canDelete(u, a) is called as a bare statement. Its boolean return is discarded, so it has no effect on control flow.
accounts.remove(id) runs regardless of the authorization result.
canDelete would return false for a non-admin who is not the owner, but that result is never checked.

finding.guards_checked: Checked canDelete (line 9-11) and its return value at the call site (line 22): not enforced. Checked assertCanDelete (line 13-17) and closeAccount (line 27-31): the correct pattern, and it is not used in deleteAccount. No route-level auth middleware or controller is in the repo, so I could not confirm the route's authentication. The bypass holds for any authenticated caller that reaches deleteAccount. Also, for a non-existent id, a is null: a non-admin hits an NPE at line 10 before removal, and an admin proceeds to accounts.remove, which is a no-op. Neither changes the finding.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) is the only authorization check in the path, and deleteAccount calls it as a bare statement at line 22 so its boolean result is discarded. The correct guard, assertCanDelete (lines 13-17), which throws, is not called in deleteAccount. No route-level auth or parameterization applies because the repo has no controller and the sink is an in-memory Map.remove. The only other check is the NPE for a missing id at line 22 when the caller is non-admin, which does not block valid ids.
verdict.reason: deleteAccount at src/AccountService.java:22 discards the canDelete result, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any caller, while closeAccount at line 29 enforces the same rule with assertCanDelete, which throws. The attacker is a non-owner, non-admin user, which is exactly the role that canDelete is meant to block, so the bypass is a real authorization flaw. Route authentication is not in the repo, but it does not change the verdict because the method's own check is what fails.
